sources.text: The paper introduces PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides non-expert users through a four-slot template (role, task, examples, output format) to write LLM prompts. It reports a within-subjects lab study with 16 university participants completing three predefined tasks (sentiment classification, topic labelling, news summarisation) under free-form and template conditions. Prompts written with the template had a higher mean automatic task score (0.74 vs 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence (4.1 vs 3.4), though they took somewhat longer. 2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples. Studies of prompt writing describe non-experts as relying on trial and error and on conversational phrasing. Prompt libraries and prompt-pattern catalogues offer reusable structures, but they are usually written for developers and have rarely been evaluated with non-expert users in a controlled setting. 3 The PromptScaffold Editor PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots. The role slot states who the model should act as. The task slot describes what to do, with a hint to name the input and the goal. The examples slot asks for one to three inputoutput pairs, and the output format slot asks how the answer should be structured. Each slot shows a short hint and an example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that the user can preview and edit freely before running it. sources.text: 1 Introduction LLM-based tools let anyone describe a task in natural language, yet writing an effective prompt remains difficult for people without machine-learning experience. Prior studies report that non-expert users tend to give instructions that are too short, rarely include examples, and leave the output format implicit. They then struggle to tell whether a poor result comes from the prompt or from the model. Structured templates are a common answer in practice, but there is little evidence on whether they help nonexperts write better prompts or only make prompts longer. This paper asks two questions. RQ1: Do prompts written with a structured template perform better on predefined tasks than free-form prompts? RQ2: How do non-expert users experience writing prompts with a template? We contribute (1) PromptScaffold, a template-based prompt editor; (2) a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants; and (3) observations on where templates help and where they constrain users. 2 Related Work Work on end-user programming shows that novices benefit from scaffolds that make implicit requirements explicit, such as forms and worked examples.
